archetype.name: Rebuilding (first-year staff)
archetype.definition: A first-year coaching staff inheriting a 3-14 roster, with a functional, ball-control offense and a pass defense that still gives up big plays to anyone with a quarterback.

report.headline: A defense that can't cover is sinking a competent, clock-eating offense
report.take:
Arizona is exactly as bad as its record says, and for a specific reason. The 2-5 start isn't bad luck: wins over expected sit at -0.14 and the point differential implies 2.1 wins, so the scoreboard and the standings agree. What drags them down is one side of the ball doing one thing badly. The defense ranks 31st in pass EPA allowed and 31st in explosive pass rate allowed, and that is why it gives up more points per game (29.7) than any team in the league. Against the run it is quite good: 9th in rush EPA allowed and 4th in missed-tackle rate. Opponents have worked that out and attack it through the air.

The offense under Jacoby Brissett, who has started all seven games, is ordinary rather than broken. It ranks 14th in success rate and 19th in EPA, protects well (8th in pressure rate allowed, 4th in short-yardage conversion, 3rd-fewest line penalties) and holds the ball, 6th in time of possession. It doesn't produce explosive plays. The run game averages 3.52 yards a carry (25th), with a 24th-ranked stuff rate, and the passing game runs through Trey McBride, whose 78 targets lead the team. The result is long drives that end in field goals, about 20 points a game, and a team that can't keep up once its secondary gives up 30.

What the averages hide is how much the passing game swings from week to week. Brissett's pass EPA ranged from +10.1 in the near-upset at San Francisco to -18.2 in the three-turnover loss to the Giants. When he is efficient they compete. When he isn't, the defense can't keep the game close. Special teams (27th in EPA per game) take away a little more each week. None of this is new. The defense ranked 26th in EPA allowed last year and 31st in 2023, so the coverage problem is a roster problem a first-year staff hasn't fixed yet.

The injury report makes the near term worse. The starting secondary is missing safety Andrew Wingard and corner Max Melton, DT Walter Nolen III and guard Jon Gaines II are out, rookie back Jeremiyah Love is working back from an ankle injury, and Jalen Brooks is done for the year. The schedule has a soft middle stretch that should produce a couple more wins, but this is a team building toward something rather than chasing a playoff spot.

strengths.title: Stout, sure-tackling run defense
strengths.body: Arizona ranks 9th in rush EPA allowed and 4th in missed-tackle rate, so running backs rarely get loose. It's a real trait of the front, not a quirk of the schedule, since it held up against good rushing teams too. The catch is that it helps less than it looks: opponents can simply throw, and the absence of DT Walter Nolen III tests the interior's depth.

strengths.title: Clean, possession-style offensive operation
strengths.body: The line keeps Brissett clean (8th in pressure rate allowed), converts short yardage at 83.3% (4th) and commits few penalties. That lets Arizona sustain drives and win time of possession, where it ranks 6th. It's a repeatable baseline that keeps them competitive in games where the defense holds up even a little.

strengths.title: McBride as the reliable focal point
strengths.body: Trey McBride's 78 targets lead the team, and tight ends get a larger share of the targets in Arizona games than the league norm. A quarterback who works the middle of the field and a tight end who wins there give the offense a floor, even without a vertical threat. With Brooks out for the year and Reiman uncertain, that concentration will only grow.

concerns.title: Coverage that leaks explosive plays
concerns.body: Arizona ranks 31st in pass EPA allowed and 31st in explosive pass rate allowed, and it's bad on short passes (29th) as well as deep ones (27th), so this isn't a single blown assignment. Opposing WR1s and WR2s both average a league-worst-tier EPA per target against it. With Melton and Wingard out, it is likely to get worse before it improves, and two straight seasons of poor defense suggest a talent gap.

concerns.title: No pass rush to cover for it
concerns.body: A 17.7% pressure rate ranks 25th, so quarterbacks get time to find the open receiver in a weak secondary. The two problems feed each other: coverage doesn't hold long enough for the rush, and the rush doesn't arrive fast enough to help the coverage. Losing Nolen on the interior thins a group that was already short of disruption.

concerns.title: Offense without a knockout punch
concerns.body: At 3.52 yards a carry with a 24th-ranked stuff rate, the run game rarely gains chunks, and the offense scores 20.3 points a game (26th). Add special teams ranked 27th and Arizona has little way to win a shootout. The ground game could get a boost if Love's ankle heals, but the ceiling here is modest.

trend.note: After the opening upset at the Chargers, Arizona has lost almost every week, mostly by two scores, with the narrow win at the Rams the exception. The offense rises and falls with Brissett's week, but the defense has given up 30-plus in most games all season.

nextGame.headline: Dallas can't defend anyone, but Arizona can't either
nextGame.body:
This sets up as a shootout between two defenses that can't stop the pass, and the Book's 54.5 total reflects it. Dallas ranks 32nd in defensive EPA allowed, 32nd in pass EPA allowed and dead last in third-down defense at 54.7%, so Arizona's patient, chain-moving offense should finally find drives that end in the end zone. The problem is the other side. Dallas runs a top-five offense by EPA with the league's lowest sack rate, against an Arizona pass rush ranked 25th in pressure and a secondary ranked 31st. Arizona gets +6.5 points, and the most likely way it covers or wins is by controlling the clock and making Dak Prescott work with fewer possessions.

Arizona's injuries are concentrated where Dallas will attack. Safety Andrew Wingard (76% of snaps) and corner Max Melton (66%) are listed out with game-day return estimates, and DT Walter Nolen III and guard Jon Gaines II are in the same spot. Their status by kickoff matters more than anything else on the report. Jeremiyah Love is listed out but expected to practice Wednesday, and if he can't go, Tyler Allgeier carries the load. Dallas is thin at linebacker, with Dee Winters (61% of snaps) out and Marist Liufau on IR, which is exactly the part of the defense McBride and the backs will test.

waysToWin.title: Feed McBride against thin linebackers
waysToWin.body: Dallas gives up 0.61 EPA per target to opposing tight ends (30th), and it is missing Dee Winters and Marist Liufau at linebacker. McBride is Arizona's most dependable option and should see heavy volume in the middle of the field. If he takes over, Arizona can move the ball without needing the explosive plays it rarely creates.

waysToWin.title: Keep Prescott on the sideline
waysToWin.body: Arizona ranks 6th in time of possession and Dallas ranks 30th, while the Cowboys let opponents convert 54.7% of third downs. Long, methodical drives shrink the number of possessions Prescott gets against a vulnerable secondary. That is the most realistic way for an underdog with a weak defense to win a high total.

waysToWin.title: Stay close and let Dallas fold late
waysToWin.body: Dallas has won only a quarter of its one-score games, is 1.39 wins under expectation and has forced just 3 takeaways all year. If Brissett plays turnover-free, Arizona can hang around into the fourth quarter, where the Cowboys have repeatedly let games slip.

waysToLose.title: Prescott picks apart a depleted secondary
waysToLose.body: Dallas ranks 7th in pass EPA, and Arizona allows explosive passes at the second-worst rate in the league. That was before Melton and Wingard got hurt. If both sit, Arizona's coverage problem becomes a mismatch, and this turns into another 30-plus allowed.

waysToLose.title: No pressure on a clean pocket
waysToLose.body: Dallas allows sacks at the lowest rate in the league (2.6%), and Arizona's pressure rate ranks 25th. Without Nolen, Prescott should have all day, which takes away the one thing that could protect a weak back end.

waysToLose.title: Brissett forced to chase the game
waysToLose.body: Arizona's offense is built for patience, and when it falls behind the passing game can collapse, as in the three-turnover, -18.2 pass-EPA loss at the Giants. An early two-score deficit takes away the run-and-control plan and leaves Brissett in obvious passing downs.

nextGame.watch: Whether Melton and Wingard make it back for kickoff. If they don't, watch how often Prescott connects on throws downfield against the backups, because that decides whether Arizona's clock control even matters.

restOfSeason.body:
The record is honest, so don't expect a bounce from luck evening out. The middle of the schedule is the reason for some optimism. After Dallas come Seattle, the Rams and Kansas City, likely the hardest stretch of the year. Then Arizona plays Washington, Philadelphia, the Jets, New Orleans and Las Vegas, mostly at home and mostly against teams with losing records and below-average defenses. An offense that moves the ball steadily should score more against those opponents, and the run defense travels to any matchup.

The pass defense is the cap. It was poor last year and the year before, and the secondary injuries suggest it won't improve soon. Expect points allowed to ease slightly from a league-worst pace as the opposing quarterbacks get weaker, not because the coverage gets fixed. A realistic finish is a handful of wins, with this season serving as a foundation-setting year for LaFleur rather than a run at the playoffs.
swingFactors: Results in the soft Weeks 12-17 stretch

confidence.note: Seven games, consistent profile, but heavy injuries in the secondary
